Title: Lightweight convolutional neural networks using nonlinear Lévy chaotic moth flame optimisation for brain tumour classification via efficient hyperparameter tuning
Text:
Lightweight convolutional neural 
networks using nonlinear Lévy 
chaotic moth flame optimisation 
for brain tumour classification via 
efficient hyperparameter tuning
Amin Abdollahi Dehkordi1, Mehdi Neshat2,3, Alireza Khosravian4, Menasha Thilakaratne4, 
Ali Safaa Sadiq7 & Seyedali Mirjalili2,5,6
Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have seen significant growth in medical image 
classification applications due to their ability to automate feature extraction, leverage hierarchical 
learning, and deliver high classification accuracy. However, Deep CNNs require substantial 
computational power and memory, particularly for large datasets and complex architectures. 
Additionally, optimising the hyperparameters of deep CNNs, although critical for enhancing model 
performance, is challenging due to the high computational costs involved, making it difficult without 
access to high-performance computing resources. To address these limitations, this study presents a 
fast and efficient model that aims to achieve superior classification performance compared to popular 
Deep CNNs by developing lightweight CNNs combined with the Nonlinear Lévy chaotic moth flame 
optimiser (NLCMFO) for automatic hyperparameter optimisation. NLCMFO integrates the Lévy flight, 
chaotic parameters, and nonlinear control mechanisms to enhance the exploration capabilities of 
the Moth Flame Optimiser during the search phase while also leveraging the Lévy flight theorem to 
improve the exploitation phase. To assess the efficiency of the proposed model, empirical analyses 
were performed using a dataset of 2314 brain tumour detection images (1245 images of brain tumours 
and 1069 normal brain images). The evaluation results indicate that the CNN_NLCMFO outperformed 
a non-optimised CNN by 5% (92.40% accuracy) and surpassed established models such as DarkNet19 
(96.41%), EfficientNetB0 (96.32%), Xception (96.41%), ResNet101 (92.15%), and InceptionResNetV2 
(95.63%) by margins ranging from 1 to 5.25%. The findings demonstrate that the lightweight CNN 
combined with NLCMFO provides a computationally efficient yet highly accurate solution for medical 
image classification, addressing the challenges associated with traditional deep CNNs.
Keywords  Convolutional neural networks (CNN), Nonlinear Lévy chaotic moth flame optimiser 
(NLCMFO), Image classification, Optimization
Medical image analysis and processing have garnered significant academic attention in the areas of disease 
detection, category classification, and progression monitoring. A brain tumour is formed by an aggregation of 
abnormal cells in the brain, leading to the development of a mass. Any growth in this region can lead to serious 
complications. Brain tumours are among the most aggressive forms of cancer, and early detection of cellular 
damage can greatly enhance treatment options and prevent potential complications for the patient1. The precise 
and careful classification of brain tumours using magnetic resonance imaging is crucial for accurate patient 
diagnosis and effective treatment planning.

The manual categorisation of brain tumors poses substantial difficulties due to significant constraints, 
including impracticality, labor intensiveness, high expenses, and lengthy time commitments. Moreover, there is 
an extensive variety of over one hundred primary types of brain tumours, each with unique symptoms, treatment 
strategies, and prognoses2. Recently, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been utilised across various 
applications, including image recognition, classification, and segmentation, yielding encouraging outcomes in 
each area. The design of CNN models is determined by hyperparameters such as the count of kernels and layers, 
the learning rate, the choice of optimiser, and the batch size, among other factors. Additionally, the number 
of hyperparameters can vary significantly among different models. The performance of CNNs is profoundly 
affected by their architectural configuration, which is closely linked to the careful selection of hyperparameter 
values. The process of fine-tuning these hyperparameters to attain their optimal values requires the expertise 
of a seasoned CNN designer, whose insights gained from each cycle of trial and error are also connected to the 
learning rate3, making hyperparameter adjustment a challenging task.
Considering that the number of hyperparameters in a CNN model is often extensive, manually adjusting an 
optimal hyperparameter setup for a CNN model designed to address real-world problems is virtually unfeasible. 
The capacity of optimal hyperparameter values to significantly enhance the performance of a CNN model4 
underscores the necessity of developing innovative strategies for optimising various hyperparameters within 
CNN systems. Optimisation plays a vital role in providing solutions to numerous real-world issues across 
various domains such as biomedicine, renewable energy, IoT, and engineering. A review of the current literature 
indicates that many metaheuristic algorithms have been designed to address similar real-world challenges4, as 
these algorithms can manage a wide array of intricate problems. Recently, numerous methodologies have been 
introduced for optimising hyperparameters within CNN models1,3,5.
The initial hyperparameter optimisation strategy concentrates on the precise tuning of hyperparameters 
within each individual layer of a CNN model, enhancing current neural networks without altering the overall 
design of the CNN model1. In contrast, the subsequent method for hyperparameter optimisation incorporates 
a broader range of parameters, such as the learning rate and the number of dense, convolutional, and max-
pooling layers, among others. This comprehensive modification range is intended to create an entirely new CNN 
model4. The current study employs an improved version of the Moth-Flame Optimisation (MFO) algorithm, 
which was originally introduced by Mirjalili in 20156. Our efforts were driven by the necessity to enhance the 
exploration and exploitation mechanisms of this algorithm to address a wider array of challenges. To achieve 
this goal, we incorporated chaotic values, the Lévy Flight Theorem, and nonlinear functions into the core 
stochastic elements of the algorithm. This integration resulted in the development of a new variant called the 
Nonlinear Lévy Chaotic Moth Flame Optimiser (NLCMFO), which provides adequate phases of exploration 
and exploitation that improve computational cost-effectiveness. The NLCMFO exhibits greater efficiency and 
effectiveness compared to MFO in exploring and exploiting search spaces relevant to problem-solving.
The efficacy of our proposed NLCMFO algorithm is evaluated through its application to a real-world 
optimisation problem and several benchmark functions. Empirical results show that NLCMFO surpassed 
the Whale Optimisation Algorithm (WOA)7, TSALSHADE8, LSHADE-SPACMA9, Multi-Verse Optimisation 
(MVO) algorithm10, MFO6, Harris Hawk Optimisation (HHO)11, Marine Predator Algorithm (MPA)12, 
Generalised Normal Distribution Optimisation (GNDO)13, Arithmetic Optimisation Algorithm (AOA)14, and 
Grey Wolf Optimiser (GWO)15 methods within the context of mathematical optimisation test scenarios.
For these reasons, within the framework of our study, we have chosen NLCMFO to improve the 
hyperparameters of CNN’s training algorithm. As a result, the methodology presented here has been designated 
as CNN_NLCMFO. In this context, the primary objective of this research effort is to optimise hyperparameters 
within a CNN framework, facilitated by a high-efficiency algorithm such as NLCMFO.
According to the existing literature, investigations focused on hyperparameter optimisation utilising nature-
inspired algorithms generally encompass several methodological steps: hyperparameter encoding, population 
initialisation, objective function formulation, pursuit of optimal solutions, and reevaluation of suboptimal 
solutions in relation to optimal results4,5. The proposed methodology aims to identify the most beneficial 
hyperparameters while simultaneously replacing the least effective parameters with the identified optimal 
alternatives.
Research into brain tumour classification faces numerous challenges. To begin with, obtaining and analysing 
medical imaging data is laden with financial and operational obstacles16. Specifically, it is often challenging to 
gather an adequate quantity and quality of training data. Additionally, uneven representation of cases from 
various categories during the classification process can adversely affect the model’s accuracy and generalisation 
capability. From a technological perspective, image databases are substantial in size and require considerable 
computational resources. These obstacles are often faced in the clinical implementation of deep learning-based 
frameworks for brain tumour classification. However, techniques such as transfer learning (TL) possess the 
potential to alleviate these issues. These methods facilitate the creation of more efficient models while utilising 
limited resources by promoting the more effective use of existing data17.
There exists a significant gap in current research focused on establishing a more precise and dependable 
classification system for brain tumours. Factors such as accuracy assessments, dataset sizes, computational 
power, uneven performance distribution, and classification categories have all surfaced as critical challenges 
in brain tumour classification. Specifically, limited datasets and computational complexities undermine the 
effectiveness of deep learning models and the proposed approach, while imbalanced performance distributions 
and a focus on certain classification types may adversely affect overall accuracy. Tackling these limitations 
necessitates an emphasis on curating larger and more representative datasets, creating more efficient algorithms, 
and employing strategies to rectify uneven performance distributions. Addressing these research shortcomings, 
which constitute the primary aim of our study, will contribute to the advancement of more accurate diagnostic 
and therapeutic strategies.

In general, researchers often prefer utilising convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures for image 
classification tasks. Within the existing literature, there is a striking lack of academic studies dedicated to 
hyperparameter optimisation aimed at boosting the performance of CNN models in the field of image 
classification. The main goal of this research is to enhance the effectiveness of a lightweight CNN, thereby 
introducing an image classification system noted for its superior performance metrics. Notably, lightweight 
CNNs are characterised by their relatively low number of layers, which eliminates the need for advanced 
computational hardware while still achieving moderate to high performance levels, as demonstrated by various 
scholarly studies. In this current research, the CNN_NLCMFO method is proposed to optimise the learning 
rate, epochs, momentum, and regularisation coefficient within the convolutional layers of lightweight CNNs, 
utilising the capabilities of the NLCMFO algorithm.
This study has yielded several noteworthy contributions that can be succinctly summarised as follows:
•	 Introduction of NLCMFO for Hyperparameter Optimisation: We have developed the NLCMFO algorithm, 
which enhances the Moth Flame Optimiser by incorporating the Lévy flight theorem, chaotic parameters, 
and nonlinear control strategies. This optimisation approach significantly improves both exploration and 
exploitation phases, thus enabling more effective hyperparameter tuning.
•	 Development of a Lightweight CNN Architecture: We have designed a resource-efficient CNN architecture 
that achieves high classification accuracy while requiring fewer computational resources compared to tradi­
tional deep CNNs. This feature is especially beneficial for medical applications where there may be limitations 
on hardware capabilities.
•	 Optimisation of Key Hyperparameters: The NLCMFO algorithm was employed to optimise critical hyper­
parameters, including the learning rate, number of epochs, momentum, and regularisation coefficient. This 
automated approach reduces the need for manual tuning, which is often time-consuming and requires con­
siderable expertise.
•	 Empirical Validation on Brain Tumour Dataset: The proposed model was subjected to a comprehensive eval­
uation using a brain tumour detection dataset, attaining a classification accuracy of 97.40%. This result rep­
resents a 5% improvement over existing CNN architectures, such as DarkNet19, EfficientNetB0, Xception, 
ResNet101, and InceptionResNetV2.
•	 Comparative Analysis with State-of-the-Art Methods: We conducted an extensive comparative analysis of 
our model against other metaheuristic-optimised CNNs and advanced transfer learning models. The results 
demonstrate that CNN_NLCMFO outperforms these approaches in terms of accuracy, stability, and reliabil­
ity.
The subsequent sections of this manuscript are structured as follows: Section "Related work" examines the 
existing literature pertaining to meta-heuristics aimed at enhancing their operational efficacy. Section "Material 
and method" provides a detailed overview of the Moth-Flame Optimisation (MFO) algorithm while assessing 
its effectiveness through graphical representations, thereby highlighting the limitations associated with both 
exploratory and exploitative search paradigms. This is followed by the introduction of an improved variant of MFO, 
designated as NLCMFO. In Section "Experimental results", we perform an evaluation of the proposed NLCMFO, 
contrasting its performance against that of the original MFO and other meta-heuristic methodologies across a 
range of well-established optimisation benchmark functions. Section "Real-world application: optimising CNN’s 
training algorithm hyperparameters" elucidates our demonstration of the proposed methodology’s effectiveness 
and efficiency through a case study centered on the optimisation of hyperparameters in Convolutional Neural 
Networks (CNNs). Finally, Section "Conclusion" concludes this paper by synthesizing our findings and outlining 
potential avenues for further research.
Related work
Meta-heuristic algorithms have received considerable interest across industries due to their success in tackling 
a wide range of real-world optimisation issues, such as single-objective, multi-objective, combinatorial, and 
limited tasks18–20. This section examines old and new meta-heuristic techniques, focusing on their practical uses 
and limitations. A main focus is on hyperparameter tuning of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which 
serves as a practical case study for our proposed Nonlinear Lévy Chaotic Moth Flame Optimiser (NLCMFO) in 
dealing with difficult, high-dimensional situations.
There are two types of optimisation methods: deterministic and stochastic. Deterministic strategies, such as 
gradient-based and non-gradient-based algorithms, are effective for linear and convex nonlinear problems, but 
they frequently fail in nonlinear, multimodal search spaces, becoming caught in local optima21–23.
The "No Free Lunch" theory underlines that no single meta-heuristic shines in all situations, encouraging 
academics to investigate various search tactics and hybrid methods to improve optimisation frameworks. 
However, even optimal algorithms require additional refinement for specific applications, and deterministic non-
gradient approaches, while commonly used, necessitate complex mathematical modeling24. On the other hand, 
deterministic (non-gradient) optimisation techniques continue to be widely utilised despite their constraints, as 
they necessitate intricate mathematical modeling for implementation25,26.
Nature-inspired meta-heuristics, drawing from biological and evolutionary processes, dominate contemporary 
optimisation research. The Genetic Algorithm (GA)27 and Harmony Search (HS)28 exemplify this trend, with 
GA leveraging mutational variables and HS focusing on harmonic components, both proving versatile across 
applications. Other evolutionary methods, such as Differential Evolution (DE)29 and Success-History-Based 
Adaptive DE (SHADE)30, alongside advanced variants like TSALSHADE8 and LSHADE-SPACMA9, further 
illustrate this diversity. These approaches often integrate sophisticated mechanisms to improve performance, 
though their effectiveness varies by problem structure.

Swarm-based metaheuristics, inspired by collective animal behaviors, have also emerged as powerful tools. 
The Bat Algorithm (BA)31 mimics echolocation, while the Spider Monkey Optimisation Technique32 reflects 
social dynamics. Algorithms like the Grey Wolf Optimiser (GWO)15, Whale Optimisation Algorithm (WOA)7, 
and Harris Hawk Optimisation (HHO)11 incorporate Lévy flight theory and chaotic values, enhancing flexibility 
and solution quality. This trend inspired the development of NLCMFO, which builds on these principles to 
optimize CNN hyperparameters, addressing the computational and performance demands of real-world 
applications like brain tumour detection.
Remarkable progress has been made in the detection of cerebral neoplasms through the use of medical 
tomography and advanced processing techniques by numerous specialists in recent years16. Both fully 
automated and semi-automated approaches have been suggested, with the acceptance of these methods in 
clinical environments often depending on the level of oversight involved in diagnostic processes33. The difficulty 
of detecting tumours using MRI image repositories remains a common challenge in the healthcare sector17, 
necessitating the creation of an MRI image categorized as either normal or abnormal for successful tumour 
detection. To achieve optimal detection results, it is crucial to utilise a comprehensive standard database for 
training classifiers and determining the most effective techniques for feature extraction and identification. The 
analysis of magnetic resonance images for the purpose of brain tumour detection is both labor-intensive and 
intricate, even for highly skilled neurologists or surgeons, due to the presence of subtle lesions that vary in 
color intensity, morphology, and texture. Misinterpretations can also occur due to distorted images or clinician 
fatigue. Quantitative image analysis, particularly through the implementation of deep learning frameworks, 
offers promising opportunities to address the shortcomings present in MRI scans. Despite its status as a relatively 
new field with a limited body of scholarly work on the subject, this section provides a brief overview of recent 
research related to the diagnosis of brain tumours using machine learning techniques34.
Balasooriya et al.35 introduced a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture specifically crafted 
to classify five different types of brain tumours through the examination of MRI imaging data. Within their 
constructed CNN framework, they achieved an impressive F1-score of 99.46% along with an accuracy rate of 
99.68%. Pashaei et al.36 carried out a classification study on a dataset consisting of three categories. Their aim 
was to utilise latent features derived from images using CNN techniques. They employed the Extreme Learning 
Machines (ELM) algorithm, which is primarily used in both classification and regression tasks. They referred 
to their method as KE-CNN and claimed that it produced promising results, reaching an accuracy of 93.68%. 
Sultan et al.37 utilised two publicly available datasets containing 3064 and 516 images, respectively, for their 
classification efforts. By employing a CNN-based deep learning architecture, they achieved a classification 
accuracy of 96.13% for the first dataset, which included three distinct classes. The second dataset was used to 
classify three grades of gliomas, resulting in an accuracy of 98.7%. Gumaei et al.38 suggested a hybrid feature 
extraction method that incorporated a regularized extreme learning machine (RELM). During the preprocessing 
stage, they applied min–max normalization to improve the contrast of brain regions and edges. Following this, 
classification was performed using RELM alongside the hybrid feature extraction method. In their experimental 
assessments, they realized an accuracy rate of 94.23% by employing the random holdout technique.
Rehman et al.39 carried out a study that introduced a computer-aided tumour detection model comprising 
three CNN architectures—VGG16, GoogLeNet, and AlexNet—equipped with transfer learning and data 
augmentation strategies to classify brain tumours. Their research revealed that the VGG16 model attained the 
highest accuracy rate of 98.69%. Although deeper convolutional neural networks can uncover more intricate 
nonlinear interactions and enhance accuracy, they frequently face challenges such as exploding or vanishing 
gradients. Similarly, Amin et al.40 utilised a stacked sparse autoencoder (SSAE) model with two fine-tuned layers 
and integrated it with a high-pass filter and median filter to detect brain tumours. However, the hyperparameter 
optimiser used in this study was not efficient in terms of speed and effectiveness. In contrast, Raj et al.41 created 
an accurate classifier for identifying brain disorders and Alzheimer’s disease using a hybrid deep learning model 
that combined a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM), optimal feature selection models (GLCM and GLRLM), 
and the Crow Search optimisation method. The proposed model exhibited superior accuracy, sensitivity, and 
specificity compared to CNN, NN, and SVM models documented by Raj et al.
Kumar et al.42 conducted a study on the classification of multi-tumour brain imaging. To address the issues of 
vanishing gradients and overfitting, they used ResNet-50 in conjunction with global average pooling approaches. 
The study used a multi-class picture dataset of 3064 images. They achieved an accuracy measurement of 97.08% 
without data augmentation, which climbed to 97.48% with the use of augmentation techniques. Irmak43 used 
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in their studies on brain tumour categorization. Three distinct CNN 
architectures were proposed in their study. Initially, they attained an impressive accuracy rate of 99.33%.
They then sorted brain pictures into five different categories with an accuracy of 92.66%. In their final 
model, the classification of brain tumours into three classes achieved an accuracy of 98.14%. Kaur et al.44 used 
the voting ensemble methodology to determine whether a brain tumour was benign or malignant. The study 
used 253 pictures from the Harvard Brain Atlas collection. Otsu segmentation was used to outline the tumour 
region in the images. The photos were processed to extract several properties such as color, texture, density, and 
shape. Classification was performed by combining the results of the Decision Trees (DT), K-Nearest Neighbors 
(KNN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithms. The classification results showed an accuracy of 
97.91%, precision of 88.89%, and sensitivity of 94.44%. Vankdothu et al.45 classified a dataset of distinct tumour 
classifications. In their study, they used Long Short-Term Memory Convolutional Neural Networks (LSTM-
CNN) for classification. It was reported that the classification of 3264 photos yielded an accuracy of 92%, a 
precision of 96%, and a recall of 98.5%.
Gupta et al.46 concentrated their efforts on detecting malignancies in brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging 
(MRI) scans. They used the InceptionResNetV2 and Random Forest (RF) models for the classification task. The 
dataset, which had 3264 photos, was augmented using Cyclic Generative Adversarial Networks. A classification

For classification, they used two-dimensional convolutional neural networks (2D CNN) and auto-encoder

the auto-encoder network. Muezzinoglu et al.52 attempted to improve the accuracy of automatic brain tumour 
categorization by employing convolutional neural networks (CNN). They developed a patch-based deep feature 
engineering model primarily for classification challenges. The study used three patch sizes: 32 × 32, 56 × 56, and 
112 × 112 with the ResNet50 architecture. They used neighborhood component analysis (NCA), ReliefF, and the 
Chi-squared (Chi2) approach to pick features. Using these techniques, they identified a total of 18 characteristics 
with k-nearest neighbors. Using the PatchResNet architecture, they achieved a classification accuracy of 98.1% in 
their analysis, which included a dataset with four separate classes. Asif et al.53 proposed a deep transfer learning

conducted a classification analysis with a dataset of 3264 MRI pictures divided into four categories. They argued 
for the use of a graph-based convolutional neural network (GCNN) during the classification phase, with a focus

Shahin et al.55 created a deep fully convolutional neural network (CNN) to aid in the classification of MRI 
images. The architecture they suggested consisted of four key modules: feature extraction, residual strip pooling 
attention, atrous spatial pyramid pooling, and classification. While these modules were combined, they achieved 
an accuracy of 0.9632, sensitivity of 0.9654, specificity of 0.9877, precision of 0.9610, and an F1-score of 0.9630

Saurav et al.56 concentrated their study on classifying multi-class MRI images using an attention-guided 
Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). They integrated channel-attention blocks to prioritize specific regions 
within the image. When analyzing a dataset comprising 3264 images, the proposed model demonstrated 
a precision of 96.33%, a recall of 95.77%, a specificity of 98.52%, an F1-score of 95.98%, and a test accuracy 
of 95.71%. Sandhiya and Raja57 investigated feature extraction from MRI images with Inception V3 and 
DenseNet201 for classification purposes. Furthermore, they retrieved radiomic characteristics to improve

tumours, gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary tumours. The Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) was used for 
categorization, which was augmented using the Particle Swarm Optimiser (PSO). Their categorization efforts 
yielded 97.97% accuracy, 98.20% precision, 97.91% recall, and an F1-score of 98.02%. Sachdeva et al.58 proposed 
a method for classifying MRI images using pre-trained Deep CNN models with ImageNet characteristics. 
Their research utilised a variety of architectures, including ResNet50, InceptionV3, Xception, DenseNet121, 
MobileNetV3Large, EfficientNetB0, EfficientNetV2L, and EfficientNetV2B0. In the output layer, the ReLU 
activation function was combined with SoftMax. Notably, EfficientNetB0 outperformed the other pretrained 
models. Using EfficientNetB0, they achieved an accuracy of 96.25% on the multi-class dataset of 3264 pictures.
The present study59 presents an adaption of the EfficientNetv2 architecture, which has been expanded and 
rescaled by incorporating the Global Attention Mechanism (GAM) and Efficient Channel Attention (ECA) to

significantly increased the model’s robustness. In general, replacing the old Multi-Layer Perceptron with

There is extensive research on the categorization and identification of brain tumours. These studies commonly 
use deep learning and machine learning techniques to classify brain magnetic resonance images16. According 
to the literature, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are very effective at classifying brain tumours. These 
models have shown adeptness in extracting features from photos and then classifying them. However, many 
studies in the available literature have distinct limitations. Certain studies have used tiny datasets62,63, which may 
limit the generalizability of the models used. Furthermore, several studies confront substantial obstacles, such as 
class imbalance, which can have a negative impact on model performance56. Some research has highlighted the 
need for preprocessing activities aimed at improving model correctness, which may unintentionally increase the 
complexity of techniques.
Binary and ternary datasets are commonly used to classify brain cancers. Binary datasets include classes 
that distinguish tumour existence and absence. Binary and ternary datasets are commonly used to classify brain 
cancers. Binary datasets include classes that distinguish tumour existence and absence. One major limitation 
associated with classification using such datasets is the inability to determine the specific tumour type64. In 
contrast, ternary datasets include classifications specific to different tumour types. The most sophisticated 
dataset type is quadrinary, which includes both brain images from healthy people and tumour diagnoses. 
Upon reviewing studies that use the same datasets, several key findings emerge. Ravinder et al.54 investigated 
the potential consequences of neglecting regional information among nearby healthy people. In previous 
studies, deep learning-based approaches performed poorly. Müezzinoğlu et al.52 achieved 98.1% accuracy 
with PatchResNet, highlighting the need for a larger dataset rather than relying on a superficial classifier. A 
review of the literature examines the strengths and flaws of existing research, which informs our investigation. 
In this framework, the use of larger and more balanced datasets is proposed to improve model performance 
and strengthen generalization capabilities. Furthermore, it is proposed that the use of more effective modeling 
techniques can improve the models’ generalizability. The identified constraints indicate the presence of a gap that 
must be closed. Inspired by these constraints, we will outline our technique and experimental endeavors in the 
following sections of this article.
A considerable amount of literature exists regarding the application of meta-heuristic methods for the 
calibration of hyper-parameters in medical deep learning frameworks. Nevertheless, a considerable fraction 
of meta-heuristic optimisers integrate control parameters that demand initialization and repeated change 
throughout the optimisation phase. The process of initializing these control parameters provides significant 
hurdles, as indicated by a high sensitivity to alterations in their initial values. Furthermore, one major worry 
about meta-heuristic algorithms’ control parameters is the lack of a smart and efficient strategy for updating 
them across most optimisation strategies. Concurrently, striking an optimal balance between meta-heuristics’ 
exploration and exploitation capacities represents another critical problem in this context.

Material and method
The MFO, Lévy Flight Theorem, and Chaotic Maps that will be used to develop our NLCMFO algorithm are 
described in this section. This algorithm’s non-linear Lévy chaotic variant is then asserted.
Moth flame optimisation algorithm
Methods based on swarm intelligence are inspired by collective intelligence in nature68. They imitate the 
behaviour of social insects, fish families, and bird flocks. These methods’ primary advantages are their flexibility 
and strength65. MFO is a population-based method developed by Mirjalili in 20156 that mimics the transverse 
orientation for navigation technique used by moths at night. Moths fly at night, relying on moonlight to guide 
them while maintaining a constant angle of attack. In this algorithm, moth behaviour is simulated as a new 
optimisation technique. Supp. Fig. 1 (see the supplementary file) illustrates a conceptual representation of this 
phenomenon.

Chaotic maps
The methods that use chaotic parameters instead of random parameters in random-based optimisation 
techniques are referred to as “chaotic optimisation algorithms (COA).” Due to the non-repetition and ergodicity 
of chaos, these algorithms can perform comprehensive searches at a higher velocity than stochastic searches that 
rely on probability24. Chaos phenomenon is a definite or undefined process that exists in nonlinear, dynamic 
(non-periodic), non-convergent, and finite processes. To do this, one-dimensional, non-invertible maps are used 
to construct chaotic sets69. As the initial variable of these chaotic maps, any number in the range [1, 0] can be 
used. It should be noted, however, that the initial value has a significant impact on the oscillation pattern of 
chaotic maps70.
Recent advancements in theoretical and practical aspects of nonlinear dynamics, particularly chaos, have 
piqued the interest of researchers in a variety of domains. The use of chaos in optimisation techniques is just one 
of those domains. During the last decade, chaotic maps have received considerable appeal from optimisation 
experts due to their dynamic characteristics. This is because chaotic maps help the optimization technique 
improve its exploration of the search space. In other words, unlike a probability-based search, the exploration

Lévy flight theory
Lévy flight, as depicted in Supp. Fig. 5 (see the supplementary file), is generally connected with small steps and, 
on rare occasions, long jumps. This property can be used to promote search efficiency in the optimisation field 
due to more efficient performance in comparison to uniform random search75. The movements from chaotic 
maps, which are plainly visible in Supp. Fig. 4, on the other hand, can explore and investigate remote portions of 
the search space but cannot search as correctly and profoundly as the Lévy approach. Thus, this study attempts to 
present an efficient optimisation method called nonlinear Lévy chaotic Moth Flame Optimisation (NLCMFO) 
that benefits from the unique characteristics of the Lévy strategy as well as features of chaotic maps. It is worth 
mentioning that a search space can be investigated and exploited both globally and locally by combining these 
methods and making use of the special characteristics of each strategy.
Nonlinear Lévy chaotic moth flame optimiser (NLCMFO)
The proposed NLCMFO is presented in this section. The primary purpose of the NLCMFO is to increase the 
performance of the standard MFO in two segments. The initial stage is to integrate MFO with Lévy flight theory 
and chaotic maps, followed by employing the nonlinear weight coefficient parameter as a control variable 
between both the algorithm’s exploration and exploitation processes.
As stated earlier in this section, MFO lacks adequate exploration and exploitation processes. Therefore, the 
primary goal of the NLCMFO algorithm is to address this obvious flaw in the MFO. In MFO, Eq. (7) simulates 
the spiral flight path of moths. The next position of a moth is defined by this equation based on the flame. In the 
spiral motion equation, the parameter t determines how close the moth’s next position should be to the flame 
(t = − 1 indicates the closest position to the flame, while t = 1 indicates the furthest distance). As a result, an excess 
ellipse can be assumed to exist in all directions around the flame, and the next position of the moth in this space. 
Spiral motion is an important component of the MFO because it determines how the moths’ positions around 
the flames are updated. It is also important to mention that each moth will be able to fly around a flame not only 
in the space between them with the help of the spiral equation, which provides this motion’s behaviour. Hence, 
utilising this type of motions, MFO could maintain both exploration and exploitation of the problem’s searching 
space. Exploration occurs in MFO when the next position is outside the moth and flame space, and exploitation 
occurs when the next position is within the moth and flame space. To emphasize exploitation even further, t is a 
random number in [a, 1]. Where a decreases linearly from − 1 to − 2 during the iterations.
The MFO’s t-parameter is critical in enhancing the algorithm’s ability to locally explore potential solutions 
to optimisation issues and in boosting the algorithm’s exploitation and exploration processes. However, as 
discussed earlier in this section, this parameter has failed to play its role in creating appropriate exploration and 
exploitation processes for the MFO. The proposed method attempts to strengthen the role of this parameter in 
improving the exploration process with the least amount of change by substituting the chaotic values produced 
by the selected chaotic maps for the random values in Eq. (8). Then, Eq. (8) is updated as follows.
	
t = |(a −1) ∗Cm + 1| 
(10)
The parameter Cm in Eq. (10) represents the chaotic values generated by the selected chaotic maps in the 
proposed method. The question that may arise here is whether it is sufficient for the moths to move towards 
the flame to update the position in Eq. (7). As a result of this process, the MFO quickly becomes stuck in 
local optimisations. To avoid this, each moth in Eq. (7) must update its position using only one of the flames. 
The flames are classified based on the fitting values obtained after each iteration and after updating the flame 
list. The moths then update their position according to the corresponding flames. The moth always updates its 
position based on the best flame on the list, while the last moth updates its position based on the worst flame 
on the list. Each moth is assigned a specific flame to prevent it from becoming trapped in the local optimum. 
Since moths can only fly towards the flame and not around it, if all of them are attracted to the same flame, they 
will all converge at some point in the search space. Forcing them to move around different flames, on the other 
hand, leads to more exploration of the search space and a lower chance of being trapped in the optimal local 
locations. According to the above, using chaotic values and modifying Eq. (8) can improve the range of motion 
of the moths and their movement around different flames, leading to improved exploratory behaviour in the 
proposed method. To increase the chances of finding better solutions, the best solutions obtained thus far are 
referred to as flames. Therefore, the F matrix in Eq. (3) always contains the n best recently obtained solutions. To 
generate chaotic values, the proposed method employs two distinct chaotic maps. Therefore, in the NLCMFO, 
if the values of the flame matrix do not change in several consecutive iterations due to the possibility of trapping 
NLCMFO in the local optimal, the chaotic values generated by the second chaotic map will be used in the next 
iteration. Moreover, this method ensures that the search space is explored in the best places obtained thus far for 
the following reasons:

Experiments were carried out to classify normal and abnormal images with tumours in order to compare 
the performance of CNN based on NLCMFO for the diagnosis of brain tumors. The network was built with 
MATLAB 2020b and runs on Windows 10 Pro with 16 GB of Nvidia GPU RAM. BRATS 201590 was used to test

A convolutional neural network with six convolutional layers is employed to classify MRI brain images. 
70% of the available data is consumed for the training phase, while the other 30% is used for network testing. 
The architecture proposed divides images into two categories: normal and abnormal (with tumours). Data 
augmentation broadens the spectrum of images inside the dataset, hence strengthening the model’s comprehension 
and increasing its flexibility in negotiating real-world complexity16. However, a substantial imbalance in the 
volume of photos across several categories has been discovered in the dataset being used. This scenario could 
lead to overfitting in classes with a high number of photos. As a result, data augmentation procedures can be 
used to increase model generalization while reducing the danger of overfitting. Data augmentation techniques, 
particularly those used in picture classification tasks, significantly improve deep learning models’ generalisation 
capabilities.
Random rotation is a popular data augmentation approach because of its ability to change image orientation. 
This approach includes applying random angle shifts to the photos. Each image in the collection is rotated at 
random, with the angle determined by a preset range. Every updated image is then used for network training, 
along with the accompanying label. Furthermore, this strategy has numerous benefits. It improves robustness 
by introducing diversity into image orientation, allowing for spatial changes and variations in viewpoint. 
Furthermore, by encouraging visual variety, it reduces overfitting while increasing generalization performance. 
In this context, the random rotation technique has been used as a data augmentation method within the study 
framework. Furthermore, the photos underwent preprocessing to improve resolution, remove noise, resize them 
to 128 × 128 × 3, and convert them to color images.

As shown in Table 8, the Adam optimiser improves accuracy compared to SGD, but the proposed CNN_

The choice to utilise stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) instead of Adam as the foundational 
optimiser in our CNN_NLCMFO framework is based on several complementary factors: Firstly, SGDM relies on 
just three essential hyperparameters—learning rate, momentum and L2Regularization—while Adam necessitates 
four (learning rate, β₁, β₂, and ε)94. By constraining the dimensionality of the hyperparameter space, NLCMFO 
can conduct a more efficient and reliable search for optimal configurations, thereby diminishing the chances of 
premature convergence and enhancing overall optimisation stability. Secondly, while Adam frequently achieves 
quicker initial convergence, empirical studies in medical imaging tasks reveal that its adaptive learning rates 
can occasionally promote overfitting and hinder generalization on unseen data. In contrast, SGDM’s uniform 
update mechanism typically delivers more consistent and resilient performance across various datasets, an 
essential attribute for clinical application. Thirdly, Adam’s per-parameter moment estimates lead to increased 
memory and computational demands—requiring the maintenance of two additional moving-average vectors—
whereas SGDM needs only one momentum term. This diminished resource requirement aligns seamlessly with 
our model’s lightweight design objectives and supports deployment on hardware with restricted memory and 
computational power, such as edge devices in point-of-care scenarios. Lastly, the relatively predictable update 
dynamics of SGDM enhance the global–local search balance of the NLCMFO algorithm. Since SGDM’s behavior 
is dictated by only a handful of controllable parameters, the metaheuristic can more transparently and effectively 
manage exploration and exploitation without the complications introduced by Adam’s adaptive schedules.
In summary, these considerations validate our selection of SGDM: by combining a straightforward yet 
dependable optimiser with NLCMFO’s robust search capabilities, we achieve exceptional classification accuracy

Discussion
The proposed CNN_NLCMFO framework highlights the potential of combining metaheuristic optimisation 
techniques with lightweight deep learning architectures to achieve enhanced diagnostic accuracy in brain tumour 
detection. By integrating nonlinear chaotic dynamics and Lévy flight strategies within the hyperparameter 
tuning framework, this model has successfully balanced computational efficiency with predictive performance. 
Such advancements are crucial in the field of medical imaging, where both accuracy and operational feasibility 
are vital for supporting effective clinical decision-making, especially in resource-limited settings. Furthermore, 
the encouraging empirical results from this study open avenues for the broader application of lightweight and 
optimally tuned CNNs across various medical imaging domains. Although this research primarily focuses on 
classifying brain MRI scans, the underlying methodology can be adapted for other imaging modalities and 
diagnostic challenges, including those associated with liver, lung, and cardiac imaging. The incorporation of 
additional interpretability layers and the validation of the model in real clinical settings are essential next steps 
for transitioning this research into practical, dependable clinical uses.
While the proposed CNN_NLCMFO framework has demonstrated notable effectiveness in detecting and 
classifying brain tumours, several limitations must be recognised to precisely define the scope, generalisability, 
and potential real-world applications of the methodology. Firstly, the evaluation of the model was performed 
solely on a single dataset consisting of 2,314 MRI images, which exhibited a relatively balanced distribution 
between tumour and normal samples. Although the achieved classification accuracy is competitive, the 
constraints imposed by the limited dataset size and its homogeneity hinder the generalisability of the results. 
In clinical settings where datasets often show a high degree of heterogeneity and significant class imbalance, 
the model’s performance may vary considerably. Moreover, the current data augmentation strategy in use 
was considered adequate due to the moderate class balance of the dataset employed. However, for more 
complex or imbalanced clinical datasets, a more advanced data augmentation technique would be necessary to 
simultaneously reduce overfitting, maintain diversity, and manage computational demands. In such scenarios, 
data augmentation becomes a multi-objective optimisation problem, where the balance between generating 
sufficient sample diversity and minimising computational complexity must be carefully maintained.
Ensuring the effectiveness of a data-driven model requires meeting certain essential conditions, which 
encompass having sufficient labeled data and maintaining consistency in the distributions of both training and 
testing datasets. However, meeting these conditions presents significant challenges in real-world situations. 
Obtaining enough labeled data often proves to be difficult, and some machines have extended lifecycles, which 
further complicates and delays the process of gathering comprehensive datasets that truly represent the entire 
lifecycle. These challenges particularly limit the practical application of machine learning techniques in fields 
such as intelligent diagnosis. Transfer learning has been developed as a method to alleviate these limitations. 
Transfer learning strategies have demonstrated successful implementations across various industries, including 
healthcare, medical image analysis, finance, and transportation systems.
Another limitation relates to the model’s lightweight CNN architecture. While its reduced computational 
complexity is beneficial for deployment in resource-constrained environments, the network’s shallow depth may 
limit its ability to extract complex hierarchical features that are essential for more challenging diagnostic tasks or 
datasets with high variability. Expanding the model for such applications may require deeper architectures and 
more sophisticated feature extraction processes, thereby partially compromising its original design simplicity. 
Additionally, the model’s reliance on optimised hyperparameters via the NLCMFO algorithm indicates that 
its application to different medical imaging tasks—such as liver or lung tumour detection or the identification 
of anomalies in other imaging modalities—would necessitate a thorough retraining and hyperparameter re-
optimisation process. Depending on the scale and intricacy of the new datasets, alterations to the network 
architecture, including the addition of extra convolutional layers, may be crucial to maintain peak performance.
The optimisation process itself, although significantly improved through the integration of chaotic maps and 
Lévy flight techniques, continues to be influenced by fluctuations in initial conditions and parameter settings. 
In spite of the substantial progress made in the exploration and exploitation aspects of the search methodology,

With respect to real-world applications, it is crucial to recognise that while the proposed framework achieves

under real operational circumstances. For effective integration into clinical workflows, further factors such 
as inference time, robustness against noise and artifacts, interpretability of model outputs, compatibility with 
hospital information systems (e.g., PACS), and adherence to regulatory standards must be carefully scrutinised. 
Although the lightweight architecture suggests potential for integration into portable or point-of-care diagnostic 
devices, these aspects were not specifically assessed in the current study and require comprehensive future 
research. Furthermore, the current lack of interpretability mechanisms—such as explainable AI features—might 
hinder clinical acceptance, highlighting another essential avenue for further improvement.
In summary, while the CNN_NLCMFO model presents a promising approach for efficient and accurate 
brain tumour detection, its widespread adoption across various clinical applications will require addressing 
challenges related to dataset diversity, augmentation strategies, model scalability, optimisation robustness, and 
validation in real-world operational scenarios.
Conclusion
This study presents the CNN_NLCMFO framework, a collaborative model that combines a lightweight 
Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with the Nonlinear Lévy Chaotic Moth Flame Optimiser (NLCMFO) 
aimed at classifying brain tumours. The model achieves an impressive classification accuracy of 97.40%, 
surpassing the performance of well-established architectures such as DarkNet19 and Xception, which both reach 
96.41%. This enhanced accuracy is especially significant in the field of medical imaging, where reliable diagnostic 
capabilities are essential for improving patient outcomes. The NLCMFO optimiser enhances the model’s 
performance by utilising chaotic dynamics and Lévy flight strategies to efficiently optimize hyperparameters, 
resulting in a solution that demonstrates computational efficiency. Such efficiency makes the model suitable for 
deployment in resource-constrained environments, positioning it as a promising tool for advancing automated 
diagnostic systems in the healthcare industry.
Building upon the strong empirical outcomes, future work will aim to extend the application of CNN_
NLCMFO to other diagnostic imaging tasks and explore integration with explainable AI components to enhance 
clinical interpretability. By addressing these future directions, this research lays a solid foundation for advancing 
automated, trustworthy, and efficient diagnostic systems within the healthcare domain.
